grade.rationale: The implementation is concise and uses deterministic JSON property ordering, ordinal comparisons, strict decoding, domain separation, and SHA-256 appropriately. However, canonicalization is incomplete when logical identifiers are duplicated, file hashing creates several full-size in-memory representations, and the manifest hash uses a different textual format from the other public hash methods.

summary: The core hashing logic is understandable and generally sound, but two canonicalization edge cases and one scalability concern should be addressed. Test coverage is unknown, so no coverage-based conclusion was drawn.

grade.rationale: Hashing and newline normalization are correct for supported encodings, but sorting does not establish a total order when duplicate logical identifiers carry different values, and hash formatting is inconsistent across the API.
The code is compact and domain-separated, although repeated manual serialization and inconsistent return conventions make future changes easier to get wrong.
Names and control flow are clear, but the API does not communicate why one hash omits the algorithm prefix or what uniqueness constraints apply to input identities.
Strict decoders correctly reject malformed input, but reading and materializing an entire file several times can cause excessive memory pressure for large files.

The pure manifest methods are straightforward to test, while file hashing is coupled directly to the filesystem. Tests should explicitly cover duplicate sort keys, encoding preambles, malformed encodings, newline variants, and large inputs.

findings.title: Canonical ordering is incomplete for duplicate identifiers
findings.description: The manifest sorts inputs only by path and selector, and the aggregate sorts members only by unit ID. If two entries share those sort keys but differ in content hash, path, or subject hash, LINQ's stable sort preserves their original relative order. Consequently, two permutations of the same logical collection can produce different hashes, despite the evident intent to canonicalize collection order.
findings.recommendation: Either reject duplicate logical identifiers explicitly or establish a total order by adding every serialized value that can differ as an ordinal tie-breaker. Add permutation tests containing duplicate primary sort keys with different payloads.

findings.title: File hashing creates multiple full-size representations in memory
findings.description: The method loads the complete file into a byte array, decodes it into a string, may allocate another string during newline normalization, and finally creates another UTF-8 byte array. A sufficiently large review subject can therefore cause disproportionate memory use or an OutOfMemoryException instead of producing a hash reliably.
findings.recommendation: Decode incrementally with a BOM-aware StreamReader or decoder, normalize line endings across buffer boundaries, and feed normalized UTF-8 data into IncrementalHash. If file sizes are intentionally bounded elsewhere, enforce and document that limit at this boundary.

findings.title: Manifest hashes use a different textual format from other hashes
findings.description: ComputeFileContentHashAsync and ComputeAggregateMembersHash return values prefixed with "sha256:", while ComputeManifestHash returns only lowercase hexadecimal characters. This makes similarly named public methods easy to misuse and can cause mismatches when their results are stored or compared through a common hash field.
findings.recommendation: Adopt one documented representation across all three methods, preferably the algorithm-qualified form, or introduce distinct value types and clearly document why manifest hashes intentionally use a different wire format. Account for compatibility if persisted hashes already exist.
